The DOL proposed a sweeping PBM transparency rule on January 30, 2026 that mandates annual audit rights with NO scope limitations for self-insured employers. Takes effect for plan years beginning July 1, 2026. Self-insured employers cover ~65% of American workers and PBMs (Express Scripts, CVS Caremark, Optum Rx) have been overcharging them for years — the FTC found the Big 3 inflate drug costs through spread pricing, rebate retention, and steering. After researching every single breakpoint in the sheet, this is the ONLY one rated VERY HIGH conviction. Why? Zero funded competitors, federal regulation creating forced buying on a hard deadline, massive dollar value (employers saving 15-30% on drug spend), and the buyers (HR/benefits teams at mid-to-large employers) have budget and urgency. Trump signed PBM reform into law on February 3, 2026 (HR 7148). DOL proposed transparency rules on January 30, 2026. PBMs must now pass through 100% of rebates, provide semiannual reporting, and give employers unrestricted audit rights. This isn't speculative legislation — it's signed law plus active rulemaking. Here's my honest take:

**Don't build all 10 for the hackathon.** You have ~7 hours until the 5 PM deadline. Building all 10 features, even as MVPs, would mean each gets ~40 minutes — you'd end up with 10 half-broken things instead of 2-3 polished ones.

**For the hackathon, build these 3 (the suggestion at the bottom of your notes is right):**

1. **Contract Intake & Parsing** — This is your "wow moment" in the demo. Upload a PBM contract PDF, AI extracts and flags clauses. Visually impressive, judges love seeing AI do something tangible.

2. **Initial Disclosure Analyzer** — Generates the gap report. This shows the *business value* — "here's what your PBM isn't telling you."

3. **Audit Request Generator** — This is the *action output*. Upload contract → see gaps → generate a legal letter. That's a complete user story in 3 clicks.

**Why not the others today:**
- Features 3-5 (semiannual auditor, rebate tracker, spread pricing) need real claims data you probably don't have. You'd be faking it.
- Features 7-8 (network adequacy, formulary manipulation) are complex data engineering problems — pharmacy network databases, formulary change tracking. Not hackathon-scoped.

Great questions. Let me research data sources for each of these features.

**Features 3-5: Semiannual Report Auditor, Rebate Passthrough Tracker, Spread Pricing Detection**

What data you need:
- **NADAC pricing** (National Average Drug Acquisition Cost) — This is **free and public**. CMS publishes it weekly at [data.medicaid.gov](https://data.medicaid.gov). It's the benchmark for what pharmacies actually pay for drugs. You can pull this via API.
- **Claims data** — This comes **from the employer customer**. When a self-insured employer signs up, they export their pharmacy claims from their PBM portal (every PBM has a claims download feature). The format varies but it's typically CSV/Excel with fields like: NDC code, drug name, quantity, days supply, amount billed, amount paid, pharmacy NPI, date filled. You don't need to source this — **your customer gives it to you**.
- **Rebate schedules** — The hard part. Manufacturer rebate amounts are **proprietary**. However:
  - SSR Health publishes estimated net prices (net of rebates) for brand drugs — subscription-based but widely cited
  - 46brooklyn Research publishes free Medicaid rebate data and drug pricing analytics
  - The new DOL rule itself **forces PBMs to disclose rebates** — so your product literally ingests what the PBM is now required to hand over
  - You can also estimate rebates using the spread between WAC (Wholesale Acquisition Cost, published by manufacturers) and actual plan-paid amounts

**For the hackathon:** Use NADAC data (free API) + generate synthetic claims data that mimics real employer claims. That's enough for a working demo.

---

**Features 7-8: Pharmacy Network Adequacy & Formulary Manipulation Detector**

- **Pharmacy network data** — The NPPES (National Plan and Provider Enumeration System) database is **free and public** from CMS. Every licensed pharmacy has an NPI number with address, phone, type. Download at [download.cms.gov/nppes](https://download.cms.gov/nppes/NPI_Files.html). ~7GB CSV but you can filter to pharmacy type codes only. You cross-reference this against employee zip codes (which the employer provides).
- **Formulary data** — CMS publishes **Medicare Part D formulary files** publicly (every Part D plan must submit them). For commercial plans, the formulary comes from the PBM/employer — again, the DOL rule now **requires PBMs to disclose formulary changes**. For detecting mid-year manipulation, you'd diff the formulary at two points in time and flag changes where the replacement drug has a higher WAC but known higher rebate.
- **Drug equivalency data** — FDA's Orange Book (free, public) tells you which drugs are therapeutically equivalent. This is how you flag "PBM swapped a $30 generic for a $300 brand" — the Orange Book confirms they're clinically interchangeable.

---

**Feature 9: Benchmarking Dashboard**

You're right that this needs volume, but there are workarounds:

1. **MEPS (Medical Expenditure Panel Survey)** — Free from AHRQ. Contains employer-level pharmacy spending data broken down by firm size, industry, and region. Not real-time but gives you baseline benchmarks.
2. **CMS Part D spending data** — Public datasets showing per-drug spending by plan. Not commercial plans, but directionally useful.
3. **HCCI (Health Care Cost Institute)** — Publishes commercial claims benchmarks. Some data is free, deeper access requires partnership.
4. **Your own customers** — Once you have 10+ employers, you anonymize and aggregate their data to build proprietary benchmarks. This is actually a **moat** — the more customers you get, the better your benchmarks, which attracts more customers. Network effect.
5. **Startup play:** Partner with a benefits broker who has 50+ employer clients. They share anonymized aggregate data, you give them the platform for free. Instant benchmark dataset.

**For the hackathon:** Use MEPS data + synthetic benchmarks calibrated to CMS published averages. Show the dashboard working with realistic numbers and explain in the pitch that production benchmarks come from customer data + broker partnerships.

---

**Summary of what's free/public vs. what comes from customers:**

| Data | Source | Cost |
|------|--------|------|
| NADAC drug pricing | CMS/Medicaid.gov | Free API |
| Pharmacy NPI registry | CMS NPPES | Free download |
| Drug equivalency | FDA Orange Book | Free |
| Employer claims data | Customer provides | Free (it's their data) |
| PBM disclosures | PBM provides (required by law) | Free (mandated) |
| Rebate estimates | SSR Health / 46brooklyn | Free–$$ |
| Benchmarks (public) | MEPS / CMS Part D | Free |
| Benchmarks (commercial) | HCCI / your own customers | Partnership |
| Medicare formularies | CMS | Free |
